q: Which compounds are converted essentially completely to their conjugate bases by one equivalent of aqueous NaOH? (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>O = 15.7)
h: Compare each O–H pK<sub>a</sub> with 15.7. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid.
w: Hydroxide removes a proton completely when the acid is much stronger than water (pKa well below 15.7). I, 4-nitrophenol (pKa ≈ 7.2): true; the phenoxide is stabilized by resonance into the ring and onto the para nitro group. II, cyclohexanol (pKa ≈ 16–18): false; an alkoxide has no resonance stabilization, so Keq with hydroxide is about 1 or less and most of the alcohol stays protonated. III, 4-methoxyphenol (pKa ≈ 10.2): true; the electron-donating OCH3 makes it slightly weaker than phenol, but it is still about 105 times stronger than water, so Keq ≈ 105.5. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the methoxy group only slightly weakens a phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10), which is still far more acidic than water.
This misjudges I: the nitro group makes the phenol more acidic, not less, so 4-nitrophenol is deprotonated even more completely.
This misjudges II: a simple alcohol has pK<sub>a</sub> near or above that of water, so NaOH does not convert it fully to the alkoxide.

q:
(R)-Octan-2-ol (shown) is treated separately with the reagents below. Which statements about the products are correct?
I. TsCl, pyridine gives the tosylate with the (R) configuration.
II. PBr3 gives (R)-2-bromooctane.
III. SOCl2, pyridine gives (S)-2-chlorooctane.
h: Ask, for each reagent, whether a bond to the stereocenter is broken. If it is, how does the halide arrive?
w: I: true. Tosylation forms the O–S bond; the C–O bond to the stereocenter is untouched, so the configuration is retained, and OTs (like OH) is the top-priority group, so the label stays (R). II: false. PBr3 turns OH into a good leaving group (–OPBr2) that bromide displaces by SN2 with inversion, giving (S)-2-bromooctane. III: true. With pyridine, SOCl2 forms a chlorosulfite that chloride displaces by SN2, again with inversion, giving (S)-2-chlorooctane. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: in pyridine, chloride attacks the chlorosulfite from the back side, so the chloride is inverted to (S).
This misjudges I: tosylation does not touch the C–O bond, so the tosylate keeps the (R) configuration.
This misjudges II: PBr3 converts a 2° alcohol by back-side SN2 attack, so the bromide is (S), not (R).

q:
Which reagents convert 3-phenylpropan-1-ol (shown) mainly to 3-phenylpropanal?
I. Na2Cr2O7, H2SO4, H2O
II. PCC, CH2Cl2
III. 1. (COCl)2, DMSO, −78 °C  2. Et3N
h: Which oxidants work without water? Water lets an aldehyde form a hydrate, which can be oxidized again.
w: A 1° alcohol stops at the aldehyde only under anhydrous conditions. I: false. Aqueous chromic acid forms the aldehyde, which hydrates and is oxidized further to 3-phenylpropanoic acid. II: true. PCC in CH2Cl2 is anhydrous, so the oxidation stops at the aldehyde. III: true. The Swern oxidation (activated DMSO, then Et3N) is also anhydrous and gives the aldehyde. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the Swern oxidation stops at the aldehyde just as PCC does.
This misjudges II: PCC in dichloromethane is the classic reagent for stopping a 1° alcohol at the aldehyde.
This misjudges I: aqueous dichromate over-oxidizes a 1° alcohol to the carboxylic acid through the aldehyde hydrate.

q:
Which combinations give 2-phenylbutan-2-ol (shown) after H3O+ workup?
I. methyl benzoate + excess CH3CH2MgBr
II. butan-2-one + C6H5MgBr
III. ethyl phenylacetate (C6H5CH2CO2Et) + excess CH3MgBr
h: Disconnect the target at the carbinol carbon. An ester plus excess Grignard puts two identical groups on that carbon.
w: The carbinol carbon of the target carries three different groups: CH3, CH2CH3 and C6H5. I: false. An ester adds two equivalents of the Grignard, so the carbinol carbon gets two ethyl groups plus the phenyl: 3-phenylpentan-3-ol. II: true. Phenyl adds to the ketone carbon of butan-2-one, which already holds CH3 and C2H5. III: false. Two methyls add to the ester carbon, which is bonded to a CH2Ph group, giving 2-methyl-1-phenylpropan-2-ol (a benzyl, not a phenyl, on the carbinol carbon). Answer: II only.
x: This misjudges I: excess ethyl Grignard adds twice to the ester, so the product has two ethyl groups and no methyl.
This misjudges III: the ester carbon of ethyl phenylacetate carries CH<sub>2</sub>Ph, so the product has a benzyl group and two methyls, not phenyl, methyl and ethyl.
This rejects the one correct route: phenyl Grignard adding to butan-2-one gives exactly the three groups the target needs.

q: Which ethers can be prepared in good yield by a Williamson ether synthesis, using the best choice of alkoxide and alkyl halide?
h: The Williamson step is S<sub>N</sub>2. For each ether, is there a disconnection that puts a methyl or primary carbon on the halide side?
w: The alkyl halide must be methyl or primary; a 2° or 3° halide with a strong alkoxide base mostly eliminates. I: false. Both sides are tertiary, so either route needs a 3° halide, which gives isobutylene by E2. II: false. Using cyclohexyl bromide (2°) with bulky tert-butoxide gives mainly cyclohexene by E2; the other route needs a 3° halide. III: true. tert-Butoxide + CH3I works because methyl iodide cannot eliminate. Answer: III only.
x: This misjudges II: the only available halide partners are a 2° halide (attacked by a bulky base, so E2) or a 3° halide (E2), so the yield is poor.
This misjudges I: di-tert-butyl ether would need a tertiary halide, which undergoes E2 with an alkoxide instead of S<sub>N</sub>2.
This misjudges I and II: each of them needs S<sub>N</sub>2 at a hindered (2° or 3°) carbon, where elimination wins.

q:
Consider the ring opening of 2,2-dimethyloxirane (shown). Which statements are correct?
I. With NaOCH3 in CH3OH, methoxide attacks the CH2 carbon of the ring.
II. With CH3OH and a catalytic amount of H2SO4, the major product is 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol.
III. Both conditions give the same constitutional isomer as the major product.
h: Under base the nucleophile does S<sub>N</sub>2 at the less hindered carbon. Under acid, which carbon of the protonated epoxide carries more positive charge?
w: I: true. A strong nucleophile opens an epoxide by SN2 at the less hindered carbon, the CH2, giving 1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol. II: true. In acid the protonated epoxide has much of its positive charge on the tertiary carbon (SN1-like transition state), so methanol attacks there, giving 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol. III: false. Because the two conditions attack different carbons, they give different constitutional isomers. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: under acid catalysis the weak nucleophile attacks the more substituted carbon, so the OCH<sub>3</sub> ends up on the tertiary carbon, which is exactly the product named.
This misjudges I: basic (S<sub>N</sub>2) opening is controlled by sterics, so methoxide attacks the unhindered CH<sub>2</sub>.
This misjudges III: base and acid give opposite regiochemistry here, so the products are constitutional isomers, not the same compound.

q:
Ethoxybenzene (shown) is heated with excess concentrated HI. Which statements are correct?
I. Iodobenzene is one of the products.
II. Phenol is one of the products.
III. Iodide attacks the ethyl CH2 carbon of the protonated ether in an SN2 step.
h: After the oxygen is protonated, which carbon can iodide reach by back-side attack: the sp<sup>3</sup> ethyl carbon or the sp<sup>2</sup> ring carbon?
w: HI protonates the ether oxygen, and iodide then attacks a carbon bonded to it. I: false. SN2 at an sp2 aromatic carbon is impossible (no back-side approach), and an aryl cation is far too unstable for SN1, so the ring C–O bond survives; phenol is not converted to iodobenzene even with excess HI. II: true. The leaving group is phenol. III: true. Iodide attacks the unhindered primary ethyl carbon, giving iodoethane. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the C–O bond that breaks is the ethyl one, by S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of iodide on the primary carbon.
This misjudges II: once iodide takes the ethyl group, the oxygen leaves still bonded to the ring as phenol.
This misjudges I: neither S<sub>N</sub>2 nor S<sub>N</sub>1 occurs at an aromatic carbon, so iodobenzene does not form.

q: Which dienes react with maleic anhydride in a Diels–Alder reaction?
h: Each diene here is held in one conformation by its ring. Is the conformation about the central single bond s-cis or s-trans?
w: A diene must be in the s-cis conformation, with C1 and C4 on the same side of the C2–C3 bond, to react. I: false. In 3-methylenecyclohexene the central bond lies in the ring, and the ring holds the exocyclic CH2 and the ring C=C on opposite sides: the diene is locked s-trans and cannot react. II: true. In 1,2-dimethylenecyclohexane both CH2 termini point the same way: locked s-cis. III: true. Cyclohexa-1,3-diene is locked s-cis by the ring. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the ring of cyclohexa-1,3-diene holds both double bonds s-cis, so it is a good Diels–Alder diene.
This misjudges II: both exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub> groups of 1,2-dimethylenecyclohexane point the same way, which is the s-cis geometry.
This misjudges I: 3-methylenecyclohexene is conjugated but locked s-trans, so its ends can never reach the dienophile together.

q: Rank compounds I–III by λ<sub>max</sub> in the UV spectrum, from shortest to longest wavelength.
h: Count the double bonds that are conjugated with each other in each compound.
w: Each added conjugated C=C narrows the HOMO–LUMO gap and moves λmax to longer wavelength. II, cyclohexa-1,4-diene, has two isolated C=C bonds (an sp3 CH2 separates them), so it absorbs below 200 nm like a simple alkene. I, cyclohexa-1,3-diene, is a conjugated diene (about 256 nm). III, octa-1,3,5,7-tetraene, has four conjugated C=C bonds and absorbs longest (near 300 nm). Order: II < I < III.
x: This puts the 1,3-diene below the 1,4-diene; the 1,4-isomer's double bonds are not conjugated, so it absorbs at shorter wavelength.
This places the tetraene below the diene; four conjugated double bonds absorb at longer wavelength than two.
This is the reverse order; longer conjugation means a longer λ<sub>max</sub>, not a shorter one.

q:
Buta-1,3-diene (shown) reacts with one equivalent of HBr. Which statements are correct?
I. At −80 °C, 3-bromobut-1-ene (the 1,2-adduct) is the major product.
II. At 40 °C, 1-bromobut-2-ene (the 1,4-adduct) is the major product because it has the more substituted, more stable C=C.
III. Both adducts form from the same resonance-stabilized allylic cation.
h: Protonate a terminal carbon and draw the resulting cation's resonance forms. Then think kinetic vs thermodynamic control.
w: I: true. At low temperature the reaction is under kinetic control; bromide bonds fastest to C2, which carries more of the positive charge (a 2° allylic carbon) and is closest to the bromide in the ion pair. II: true. At higher temperature the additions are reversible, so the more stable product wins: the 1,4-adduct has a disubstituted C=C, while the 1,2-adduct has a monosubstituted one. III: true. Protonation at C1 gives one allylic cation with positive charge shared by C2 and C4; attack at C2 gives the 1,2-adduct and attack at C4 the 1,4-adduct. Answer: I, II, and III.
x: This misjudges III: there are not two separate cations; one allylic cation with two resonance forms leads to both products.
This misjudges II: under equilibrating (warm) conditions the 1,4-adduct dominates because of its more substituted double bond.
This misjudges I: at −80 °C the faster-forming 1,2-adduct is the major product.

q:
(2E,4Z,6E)-Octa-2,4,6-triene (shown) undergoes 6π electrocyclic ring closure. Which statements are correct?
I. The thermal ring closure is disrotatory.
II. The thermal product is trans-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene.
III. The photochemical ring closure is conrotatory.
h: Find the HOMO of a hexatriene in the ground state (ψ<sub>3</sub>) and in the excited state (ψ<sub>4</sub>), and look at the phases of the end lobes.
w: I: true. A 6π (4n + 2) system closes thermally from its ground-state HOMO, ψ3, whose terminal lobes have the same phase on the same face, so the ends rotate disrotatory. II: false. With E,Z,E geometry both terminal methyls point outward; disrotatory closure turns both outward groups the same way, putting them on the same face: cis-5,6-dimethylcyclohexa-1,3-diene. III: true. Light promotes an electron to ψ4, whose terminal lobes are out of phase, so the photochemical closure is conrotatory (and would give the trans product). Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: in the excited state the HOMO is ψ<sub>4</sub>, which has opposite end-lobe symmetry, so the photochemical closure is conrotatory.
This misjudges I: a thermal 6π electrocyclization is disrotatory, not conrotatory (conrotatory is the thermal mode for 4π systems).
This misjudges II: disrotatory closure of the E,Z,E triene gives the cis-dimethyl ring; the trans isomer is the photochemical product.

q: Which of these ions are aromatic? (Assume each ring is planar.)
h: Count π electrons: each C=C gives 2, a carbocation's empty p orbital gives 0, and a carbanion's lone pair gives 2. Then apply 4n + 2.
w: Each ring is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, so the π-electron count decides. I: cyclopropenyl cation, one C=C and an empty p orbital: 2 π electrons (4n + 2, n = 0), aromatic. II: cyclopentadienyl cation, two C=C and an empty p orbital: 4 π electrons (4n), antiaromatic. III: cycloheptatrienyl anion, three C=C and a lone pair: 8 π electrons (4n), antiaromatic. Answer: I only.
x: This misjudges II: the cyclopentadienyl cation has 4 π electrons, a 4n count, so it is antiaromatic. (The cyclopentadienyl anion, with 6, is the aromatic one.)
This misjudges III: the cycloheptatrienyl anion has 8 π electrons, a 4n count. (The cation, tropylium, with 6, is the aromatic one.)
Only the cyclopropenyl cation has a 4n + 2 count; the other two ions have 4 and 8 π electrons and are antiaromatic.

q: Which of these heterocycles are aromatic?
h: First check that every ring atom has a p orbital. Then count π electrons, using one lone pair from the heteroatom if it is needed.
w: I: false. 4H-Pyran has an sp3 CH2 in the ring, which breaks the cyclic conjugation, so it is not aromatic. II: false. 1H-Azepine has three C=C bonds plus the N lone pair, 8 π electrons (4n); a planar ring would be antiaromatic, so the ring puckers and is nonaromatic. III: true. Furan has two C=C bonds plus one oxygen lone pair in a p orbital, 6 π electrons in a planar ring. Answer: III only.
x: This misjudges II: using the nitrogen lone pair, azepine has 8 π electrons, a 4n count, so it cannot be aromatic.
This misjudges I: the sp3 CH2 of 4H-pyran has no p orbital, so the ring is not fully conjugated.
This misjudges I and II: one has an sp<sup>3</sup> ring carbon and the other has 8 π electrons, so only furan meets Hückel's rule.

q: Rank these heterocycles in order of increasing basicity (weakest base first).
h: For each, find a lone pair that is NOT part of the aromatic sextet. Then ask whether the protonated form gains extra stabilization.
w: I, pyrrole: its only nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, so protonation (which occurs at carbon) destroys aromaticity; pKa of the conjugate acid ≈ −4. Weakest. III, pyridine: the lone pair sits in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, outside the π system, so it is available; pKaH ≈ 5.2. II, imidazole: the pyridine-like N3 has an available sp2 lone pair, and the cation formed is symmetric, with the positive charge shared equally by both nitrogens through resonance; pKaH ≈ 7.0. Strongest. Order: I < III < II.
x: This puts pyridine above imidazole; the imidazolium ion is stabilized by resonance over two nitrogens, so imidazole is the stronger base by about 2 pK<sub>a</sub> units.
This puts pyrrole above pyridine; pyrrole's lone pair belongs to the aromatic sextet, so it is a far weaker base than pyridine.
This is the reverse order; pyrrole, with no available lone pair, is the weakest base, not the strongest.

q: Which of these ions are aromatic? (Assume each ring is planar.)
h: Count π electrons in each planar ring and test 4n + 2. A carbanion lone pair counts 2; a carbocation counts 0.
w: I: true. The cyclooctatetraene dianion has three C=C bonds plus two carbanion lone pairs, 10 π electrons (n = 2): aromatic, and it is in fact planar. II: true. The cyclononatetraenyl anion has four C=C bonds plus one lone pair, 10 π electrons: aromatic. III: false. The cyclononatetraenyl cation has four C=C bonds and an empty p orbital, 8 π electrons (4n): antiaromatic. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: four C=C bonds plus the carbanion lone pair give 10 π electrons, a 4n + 2 count.
This misjudges I: the two negative charges add two lone pairs to the six π electrons of the C=C bonds, giving 10, which is aromatic.
This misjudges III: the cation has only 8 π electrons because the cationic carbon contributes an empty p orbital.

q:
Consider Birch reduction (Na, NH3(l), CH3CH2OH). Which statements are correct?
I. Benzene gives cyclohexa-1,4-diene.
II. Anisole (shown first) gives a diene in which the OCH3 group is on an sp3 carbon.
III. Benzoic acid (shown second) gives a diene in which the CO2H group is on an sp3 carbon.
h: Birch reduction adds electrons to the ring. Does an electron-donating group sit on a reduced carbon or stay on a C=C? What about an electron-withdrawing group?
w: I: true. Birch reduction adds two electrons and two protons to para positions, leaving the nonconjugated cyclohexa-1,4-diene. II: false. An electron-donating group avoids the carbons that pick up negative charge, so it stays on a ring double bond: anisole gives 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene, with OCH3 on an sp2 carbon. III: true. An electron-withdrawing group stabilizes the negative charge, so its carbon is reduced: benzoic acid gives cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1-carboxylic acid, with CO2H on the sp3 carbon. Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: an electron-withdrawing group ends up on a reduced (sp<sup>3</sup>) carbon, because it stabilizes the radical anion and carbanion there.
This misjudges I: Birch reduction of benzene gives the 1,4-diene, not a conjugated diene and not cyclohexane.
This misjudges II: an electron-donating group like OCH<sub>3</sub> stays on a C=C after Birch reduction.

q: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, which of these compounds direct the incoming electrophile mainly to the ortho and para positions?
h: Is the atom bonded to the ring carrying a lone pair it can donate by resonance into the arenium ion?
w: An o/p director has an atom with a lone pair (or an alkyl group) attached to the ring, which stabilizes the ortho and para arenium ions. I: false. CF3 has no lone pair on the attached carbon and withdraws strongly by induction, so it is a deactivating meta director. II: true. Chlorine deactivates by induction but donates a lone pair by resonance, so it directs o/p. III: true. In phenyl acetate the ring is bonded to the ester oxygen, whose lone pair donates into the ring; it is a moderately activating o/p director (unlike methyl benzoate, where the carbonyl carbon is attached). Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: the ring carbon of phenyl acetate is bonded to an oxygen with lone pairs, so the group is o/p directing, not meta.
This misjudges II: halogens deactivate the ring yet still direct o/p through lone-pair resonance.
This misjudges I: the CF<sub>3</sub> group has no lone pair to donate and pulls electron density away, so it directs meta.

q: Rank these compounds by rate of nitration with HNO3/H2SO4, from slowest to fastest.
h: Each nitro group strongly withdraws electron density. How does a halogen compare?
w: The rate of EAS falls as the ring loses electron density. I, 1,3-dinitrobenzene, carries two strongly deactivating nitro groups and is slowest. II, nitrobenzene, has one. III, fluorobenzene, is only weakly deactivated (F withdraws by induction but donates a lone pair by resonance) and reacts nearly as fast as benzene. Order: I < II < III.
x: This puts one nitro group below two; each nitro group deactivates further, so the dinitro compound is slowest.
This is the reverse order; nitro groups slow EAS, so the dinitro compound is slowest, not fastest.
This puts fluorobenzene below nitrobenzene; a halogen deactivates only weakly, while a nitro group deactivates strongly.

q:
Which statements about Friedel–Crafts reactions are correct?
I. Benzene with 1-chloropropane and AlCl3 gives mainly isopropylbenzene.
II. Friedel–Crafts acylation stops after one acyl group is added because the aryl ketone product is deactivated.
III. Nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts alkylation or acylation.
h: Think about what the electrophile is in each reaction, whether it can rearrange, and how reactive the ring must be.
w: I: true. The 1° chloride–AlCl3 complex undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable 2° (isopropyl) carbocation, so isopropylbenzene is the main product (the classic rearrangement problem of alkylation). II: true. The acyl group withdraws electron density by resonance, so the product ring is less reactive than benzene and does not react again; this is why acylation avoids the polysubstitution seen in alkylation. III: true. Friedel–Crafts reactions fail on rings more deactivated than a halobenzene, and nitrobenzene is so unreactive it is even used as a solvent for them. Answer: I, II, and III.
x: This misjudges III: a strongly deactivated ring such as nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions at all.
This misjudges I: the primary propyl electrophile rearranges by a hydride shift, so isopropylbenzene, not propylbenzene, is the main product.
This misjudges II: the ketone product is deactivated, which is exactly why acylation, unlike alkylation, stops after one substitution.

q:
Which sequences, starting from benzene, give 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene (shown) as the major product?
I. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. Br2, FeBr3
II. 1. Br2, FeBr3  2. HNO3, H2SO4
III. 1. HNO3, H2SO4  2. NBS, hν
h: The group already on the ring decides where the second group goes. Which group must be on first to direct meta?
w: The two groups are meta, so the first group must be a meta director. I: true. Nitrobenzene is brominated (Br2/FeBr3) at the meta position. II: false. Bromine is an o/p director, so nitrating bromobenzene gives mainly 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene (with some ortho), not the meta isomer. III: false. NBS with light brominates benzylic or allylic C–H bonds by a radical path; nitrobenzene has no such position and NBS does not perform ring EAS here. Answer: I only.
x: This misjudges II: bromine directs o/p, so the nitro group goes para or ortho to it, not meta.
This misjudges III: NBS/hν is a radical benzylic bromination, and nitrobenzene has no benzylic hydrogens.
This reverses the logic: brominating first gives the wrong (o/p) pattern, while nitrating first gives the meta product.

q: Which aryl halides react readily with NaOCH<sub>3</sub> in CH<sub>3</sub>OH (mild heating) by nucleophilic aromatic substitution (addition–elimination)?
h: Add methoxide to the carbon bearing the halogen and draw the anion. Can the negative charge reach the oxygens of a nitro group?
w: SNAr goes through an anionic (Meisenheimer) intermediate whose charge sits ortho and para to the attacked carbon, so a nitro group must be ortho or para to the leaving group. I: false. The nitro group is meta to Cl, so it cannot delocalize the charge by resonance. II: true. The nitro group is para to F; fluoride is an excellent SNAr leaving group because its electronegativity speeds the rate-determining addition step. III: true. Nitro groups ortho and para to Cl both stabilize the intermediate. Answer: II and III only.
x: This misjudges III: two nitro groups ortho and para to the chlorine make 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene highly reactive in S<sub>N</sub>Ar.
This misjudges II: a para nitro group activates the ring, and fluoride is the best halide leaving group in S<sub>N</sub>Ar, not the worst.
This misjudges I: a meta nitro group cannot accept the negative charge by resonance, so the ring is not activated.

q: Rank these carbonyl compounds by the equilibrium constant for hydrate formation in water, from smallest to largest.
h: Hydration is favored when the C=O carbon is very electron-poor and when converting it to sp<sup>3</sup> costs little steric strain.
w: Alkyl groups donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon and crowd the sp3 hydrate, so they shift the equilibrium toward the carbonyl. I, acetone, has two alkyl groups: K ≈ 10−3, smallest. III, propanal, has only one alkyl group and an H: K ≈ 1. II, 1,1,1-trifluoroacetone, is a ketone, but the strongly electron-withdrawing CF3 group destabilizes the C=O and favors the hydrate: K well above 1, largest. Order: I < III < II.
x: This puts the aldehyde below the ketone acetone; an aldehyde has one fewer donating alkyl group and less steric crowding, so it hydrates more.
This puts the trifluoromethyl ketone below the aldehyde; the CF<sub>3</sub> group's strong inductive withdrawal outweighs the extra substituent and drives hydration.
This is the reverse order; acetone has the least electrophilic carbonyl and the smallest hydration constant.

q:
Which reagents reduce the ketone carbonyl of methyl 4-acetylbenzoate (shown) to a CH–OH group while leaving the ester unchanged?
I. 1. LiAlH4, ether  2. H3O+
II. NaBH4, CH3OH, 0 °C
III. Zn(Hg), HCl, heat
h: Rank the reagents by hydride strength, and remember that one of these reagents removes the oxygen completely.
w: I: false. LiAlH4 is strong enough to reduce both carbonyls, so the ester also becomes a CH2OH group. II: true. NaBH4 reduces ketones and aldehydes readily but esters only very slowly, so it gives methyl 4-(1-hydroxyethyl)benzoate. III: false. The Clemmensen reduction converts the ketone C=O all the way to CH2 (an ethyl group), not to an alcohol. Answer: II only.
x: This misjudges I: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> also reduces the ester to a primary alcohol, so it is not selective.
This misjudges III: Zn(Hg)/HCl removes the carbonyl oxygen entirely, giving CH<sub>2</sub>, not CH–OH.
This misjudges I and III: one reduces the ester as well, and the other deoxygenates the ketone to CH<sub>2</sub>.

q:
Cyclohexanone (shown) is treated with each reagent below and a catalytic amount of acid, with removal of water. Which give a product containing a C=N bond?
I. CH3NH2
II. (CH3)2NH
III. NH2OH
h: After the iminium ion forms, does the nitrogen still have an H it can lose?
w: A primary amine (or another NH2 compound) condenses with a ketone to an iminium ion that loses its N–H proton to give a neutral C=N. I: true. Methylamine gives the N-methyl imine. II: false. Dimethylamine is secondary; its iminium ion has no N–H to lose, so it loses an α C–H instead and forms an enamine (C=C–N), with no C=N in the neutral product. III: true. Hydroxylamine has an NH2 group and gives an oxime (C=N–OH). Answer: I and III only.
x: This misjudges III: hydroxylamine condenses through its NH<sub>2</sub> group to give an oxime, which contains a C=N bond.
This misjudges I: a primary amine such as methylamine gives an imine, the standard C=N product.
This misjudges II: a secondary amine cannot form a neutral C=N, so it gives an enamine instead.

q:
Which Wittig combinations give methylenecyclohexane (shown)?
I. cyclohexanone + Ph3P=CH2
II. formaldehyde + the ylide Ph3P=C(CH2)5 (cyclohexylidene)
III. cyclohexanecarbaldehyde + Ph3P=CH2
h: The Wittig reaction joins the carbonyl carbon and the ylide carbon with a C=C. Split the target's C=C into those two halves.
w: Cutting the target's C=C gives two halves: a CH2 and a ring carbon. Either half can come from the carbonyl and the other from the ylide. I: true. Cyclohexanone supplies the ring carbon and the methylene ylide supplies CH2. II: true. Formaldehyde supplies CH2 and the cyclohexylidene ylide supplies the ring carbon (a less common but valid route). III: false. The aldehyde carbon is outside the ring, so the new C=C is too: the product is vinylcyclohexane, an isomer of the target. Answer: I and II only.
x: This misjudges II: reversing the roles (formaldehyde plus the ring ylide) forms the same C=C bond.
This misjudges I: cyclohexanone with Ph<sub>3</sub>P=CH<sub>2</sub> is the textbook route to methylenecyclohexane.
This misjudges III: the carbonyl carbon of cyclohexanecarbaldehyde is exocyclic, so the product is vinylcyclohexane, not methylenecyclohexane.
